_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss (Peter's wife vs Sofia's grandmother; Amira helping vs Sofia making). Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 4.
title: A weekend to remember
subtitle: Four people describe a festival that turned out differently from what they expected.

sections.A: Joe, 23, music festival. Four of us had bought tickets months in advance, and then, one by one, the others dropped out: a wedding, an exam resit, a broken ankle. I very nearly sold mine. In the end I went by myself, which felt slightly sad on the train and not at all sad by the evening. It rained for three days without stopping, the field turned into something closer to a swamp, and on the second night my tent quietly collapsed while I was out. None of it mattered. I spent that night in a stranger's tent with five people I'd met in a queue for coffee, and we still have a group chat that's busier than any of my others. I missed most of the bands I'd paid to see, and I'd do every minute of it again.
sections.B: Amira, 31, food festival. I signed up as a volunteer at a seafood festival on the coast, mainly because it got me in free; the tickets were ridiculously expensive for what was, essentially, a car park full of food stalls. I spent two days directing traffic and collecting rubbish, which was about as glamorous as it sounds. On the last afternoon, though, a chef giving a cookery demonstration was short of a helper, and I was sent over. For an hour I chopped, passed things and watched someone who clearly loved what she did. I went home and, for the first time in years, seriously asked myself whether I wanted to spend the rest of my life in an office. I haven't regretted it once. I'm now halfway through a part-time course in professional cookery.
sections.C: Peter, 58, book festival. I went to a book festival for the first time three years ago, entirely because my wife wanted to go and didn't want to drive. I'm not much of a reader, and I took a newspaper to hide behind. Then we went to a talk by a novelist I'd never heard of, who described her father's farm in a way that reminded me so much of my own childhood that, at the end, I put my hand up. I hate speaking in public, and my voice shook all the way through the question. She answered it beautifully, and afterwards she signed a copy of her book for me. I've read everything she's written since. We've been back every year, and these days I'm the one who books the tickets.
sections.D: Sofia, 19, lantern festival. Every autumn my grandmother's village holds a lantern festival, and every autumn as a child I was taken there, whether I liked it or not. As a teenager I found the whole thing deeply embarrassing: the singing, the paper lanterns, the old men giving speeches nobody listened to. Last year, for the first time, nobody made me go. I went anyway, and I even spent a week making my own lantern from bamboo and rice paper, following instructions my grandmother wrote out for me. Walking through the dark streets with it, behind a few hundred neighbours, I suddenly understood why she had insisted all those years, and I was glad she had. It isn't really about the lanterns. It's about who's walking next to you.

questions.question: Which person ended up going alone after others changed their plans?
questions.why: 'One by one, the others dropped out… In the end I went by myself.' Peter went with his wife.

questions.question: Which person worked at the event rather than simply attending it?
questions.why: She was 'a volunteer', 'directing traffic and collecting rubbish'.

questions.question: Which person went the first time mainly to please someone else?
questions.why: 'Entirely because my wife wanted to go.' Sofia was taken as a child, but she went by choice last year, the visit she describes.

questions.question: Which person was made to question their career by what they saw?
questions.why: Watching the chef, she asked 'whether I wanted to spend the rest of my life in an office', and is now training as a cook.

questions.question: Which person overcame nerves to speak in front of others?
questions.why: 'I hate speaking in public, and my voice shook all the way through the question.'

questions.question: Which person now feels differently about the event from how they felt when younger?
questions.why: As a teenager she found it 'deeply embarrassing'; now she 'understood why she had insisted'.

questions.question: Which person did not let uncomfortable conditions spoil the experience?
questions.why: Rain, a swamp and a collapsed tent: 'None of it mattered.'

questions.question: Which person thought the event was poor value for money?
questions.why: 'The tickets were ridiculously expensive for… a car park full of food stalls.'

questions.question: Which person made something to take part in the event?
questions.why: She spent a week 'making my own lantern from bamboo and rice paper'. Amira helped a chef, but did not make anything for herself.

questions.question: Which person has taken over the organising of a regular visit?
questions.why: 'We've been back every year, and these days I'm the one who books the tickets.' Joe would go again but says nothing about organising.
